quote: If editing becomes available only to the wealthy, some fear a society stratified not just by money but by biology, in which advantages are literally inherited. Disability communities have offered some of the most searching critiques: many deaf people, people with dwarfism and others argue that their lives are rich and valuable, and that a drive to edit out their conditions sends a painful message that people like them should not exist. They ask whether money spent on editing might be better spent on inclusion, services and cures for suffering rather than elimination of difference. This history carries particular weight in Australia, where eugenic ideas once justified the forced removal of Aboriginal children and other grave injustices. First Nations people also raise distinct concerns about genetic research conducted without consent and about who controls Indigenous genomic data. These memories make many Australians alert to how quickly "improving" populations can become oppressive.
